newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Malaysia asks banks to cap base lending rate.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Malaysia asks banks to cap base lending rate.

text.p: Malaysia's central bank has asked commercial banks to hold their base lending rates (BLR) steady despite the recent spike upward in interbank rates, banking sources said on Friday.
They said a circular on the matter was distributed to banks on Thursday.
The BLR -- the interest rate banks offer to their best clients for loans -- is a key rate used as a benchmark for other commercial rates.

Under a new formula announced in October 1995, calculation of BLR is pegged to the average three-month Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rate (KLIBOR) over a month. Bank Negara Malaysia, the central bank, then fixed a ceiling rate for BLR.
The BLR ceiling in July was fixed at 9.67 percent, unchanged from June.
Money market dealers said based on the formula, the ceiling for July should be at 10.06 percent.
With the exception of Malayan Banking, banks are now quoting base lending rates at between 9.50 and 9.65 percent.
Malayan Banking, Malaysia's largest bank, last month raised its rate to 9.35 percent from 9.10 percent.
Economists believe Bank Negara is trying to prevent BLR from crossing the psychological 10 percent level.
"Anything above 10 percent is a scary number," said Kostas Panagiotou, a senior economist at Kim Eng Securities.
Economists said the move by the central bank indicates that interest rates in Malaysia are heading lower.
"Bank Negara will have to bring rates down," said Jimmy Koh, an economist at I.D.E.A. in Singapore. "If not, banks will suffer and will likely pass on the cost of funding to corporates."
Analysts had earlier said that the recent surge in interbank rates would lead to another round of increases in base lending rates this month.

Interbank rates rose sharply in July, triggered by a sudden tightening of liquidity in the system as a result of Bank Negara's massive intervention in the foreign exchange market to defend the ringgit from a speculative attack.
The dollar sales by the central bank mopped up six to eight billion ringgit from the market, leaving the domestic banking system heavily short of funds.
Interest rates shot through the roof on July 10, two days after the Bank Negara intervention.
The overnight interbank rate hit 50 percent, from its normal levels of 5.5 to 8.5 percent. One-month money traded for the next few days between 15 and 20 percent.
Economists said after unsuccessfully defending the ringgit, Malaysia is shifting its focus to keeping domestic interest rates stable to achieve growth.
"The authorities are obviously concerned about the impact of high interest rates on the economy. High interest rates will have a dampening effect on domestic spending," said Panagiotou.
Dealers and economists said one probable move to bring down interbank rates was to lower the statutory reserve requirement (SRR) of banks and other financial institutions.
SRR is a certain percentage of a bank's deposits it has to keep with the central bank, interest free. It was raised to 13.5 percent from 11.5 last year.
But a more viable option is for Bank Negara to continue injecting funds into the money market, they said.
The central bank has been lending one-month money over the past two weeks.
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-201 4813)
